932.hook: riots sweep Spain; people are killed and others forced to convert
932.carry: remembered, by name and by place
932.howItsDone: Jews remember the persecutions of Spain in study and in memorial gatherings, and some descendants of conversos today explore and recover their family's Jewish history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zohar. Your line was the book of radiance. Today the light in Spain goes dark, and we take it slowly.

City by city, a father lists what has happened. He is writing to Jews in another country: Hasdai Crescas, a philosopher and a community leader in Aragon, with a duty to report. He names it all: the mobs, the burned streets, the people killed, the people dragged to the font and baptized under threat. Partway through, he writes about Barcelona, and about his own son, killed there. The letter is careful, almost formal, and then it is not. Today's lesson has a year for its name: thirteen ninety-one.
screen: `A FATHER WRITES A REPORT.` → `CITY BY CITY.` → `HIS OWN SON, IN BARCELONA.`

segments.voice: It started in Seville. For some time a church official there, Ferrand Martínez, had been preaching against the Jews of the city, against the wishes, records say, of some above him. When the moment came, crowds broke into the Jewish quarter. From there the violence ran along the roads, through Castile and into Aragon, town after town, through the summer. Some local rulers tried to protect Jewish quarters; others could not or did not. Crescas's letter is one of the witnesses, and it names two kinds of loss: the dead, and the living who were forced, at the edge of a sword, to accept baptism. That second loss is the one this day asks us to hold. In Hebrew the forced ones are called anusim. Those who converted, under threat or under years of pressure, became known in Spain as conversos, New Christians. Some held on to Jewish customs in secret, lighting a candle on Friday behind closed shutters. Some became sincere Christians. Other families were somewhere in between, and were looked at with suspicion by both sides. Jewish law starts from a principle the Rambam's code sets down: a person forced is not judged like a person who chooses. Later rabbis argued hard over those who stayed Christian when they might have left. And the communities that survived kept going, rebuilding synagogues and teaching their children, though Spain would never again be what it had been. This is not a story to turn into a slogan. It is a story to be remembered, carefully, by name and by place.
screen: `IT STARTED IN SEVILLE.` · `THE KILLED AND THE FORCED.` · then, large: `ANUSIM: THE FORCED ONES.` · `REMEMBERED BY NAME AND PLACE.`

Picture one small thing they might have kept, a candle behind a shutter, a recipe passed down without its reason, and stay with them. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words; if you don't, simply hold them.

933.title: Rabbeinu Gershom
933.hook: his rulings ban polygamy and opening other people's letters
933.howItsDone: Ashkenazi communities accepted the decrees of Rabbeinu Gershom, and they still shape Jewish marriage and divorce law today; some people still write a short Hebrew reminder of the ban on reading others' letters on the envelope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thirteen ninety-one and the anusim. Your line was remembered, by name and by place. Today we go north to the Rhine, to Ashkenaz.

Who owed whom, who was ill, who was in trouble: a courier's pouch riding between two river towns could tell you all of it. Inside are business deals, family news, a marriage arranged, a legal question for a rabbi. In a small community, that kind of knowledge is power. Now set a rabbi of Mainz beside that pouch, and hear the rule tradition gives him: no one may open a letter that isn't theirs. Not the courier, not the curious neighbor. He makes it a binding rule, with the community's full weight behind it. Today, the teacher Ashkenaz remembers as the light of the exile.
screen: `A POUCH OF LETTERS.` → `KNOWLEDGE IS POWER.` → `NO ONE MAY OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: Rabbeinu Gershom means our teacher Gershom. He taught in Mainz, one of the Rhine towns we met earlier, and his students went on to teach across the region. Later generations called him Me'or HaGolah, the light of the exile. His name is attached to a set of community decrees, called takkanot, backed by a herem, a ban: break it and you could be shut out of community life. Tradition attributes several to him, and scholars debate which ones really go back to him. Three stand out. First, a man may not take more than one wife. The Torah's stories include men with several wives; this decree closed that door in the communities that accepted it. Second, a husband may not divorce his wife against her will. Put those two together and a wife's place became far more secure. Third, today's line: no one may read a letter addressed to someone else. Privacy, written into law. And one more teaching tradition ties to his name, gentle and fitting after yesterday: when someone who had been forced to convert came back to the community, no one was to shame them by bringing up their past. Notice what links these decrees. Each protects someone with less power: the wife, the letter writer, the returning convert. A rabbi in a small northern town looked at ordinary life and drew lines around the people who could be hurt in it.

934.title: Rashi's life
934.hook: a winemaker in Troyes who explained the Bible and Talmud
934.howItsDone: Jews studying the weekly Torah portion often read it with Rashi's commentary, and his notes appear on the inner margin of the printed Talmud page.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbeinu Gershom, the light of the exile. Your line was don't read their letters. Today, a student of his students, in France.

A printed page of the Torah, the kind used for study. Look at the column beside the verses: small letters, a slightly different shape from the main text. Open a page of the Talmud, and there it is again, on the inner margin, close to the spine. The same voice on both, explaining a word here, a sentence there, answering the question a beginner was about to ask. That voice belongs to a man from a market town in Champagne, in France. He was a scholar. And tradition says he also worked with vines. Today, Rashi's life.
screen: `A COLUMN BESIDE THE VERSES.` → `THE SAME VOICE ON THE TALMUD.` → `A TOWN IN CHAMPAGNE.`

segments.voice: Rashi is a name from initials: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, Solomon son of Isaac. He was from Troyes. As a young man he went to study in the Rhine towns, Mainz and Worms, with teachers who had learned from the circle of Rabbeinu Gershom. Then he came home and opened a school. Tradition says he made his living from vineyards, and readers point to how well his commentary knows pressing grapes and handling wine. Some historians ask whether that's a memory or a guess; the commentary itself is the evidence people bring. What he wrote is the point: the plain meaning of the Torah and the Talmud, word by word, for anyone sitting down to learn. Take the first verse. In the JPS translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Rashi's first comment asks a student's question. If the Torah is a book of commandments, why doesn't it start with the first commandment given to Israel as a people, in Exodus? Why start with creation? He answers with a teaching of the rabbis: the story of the world comes first, because the whole earth belongs to God, who gives each land to whom God chooses. Notice the habits. He uses the French of his town, written in Hebrew letters, to explain hard words. He says when he doesn't know. And he writes briefly. His commentary is still printed beside the text: a man who, tradition says, lived by his town's ordinary trade, and made the hardest books readable.

935.title: Rashi's daughters
935.hook: tradition remembers them as learned; his grandsons began the Tosafist school
935.howItsDone: Students of the Talmud read each passage with Rashi on the inner margin and the Tosafot on the outer margin, and in some communities today girls and women study these same pages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi's life. Your line was vintner and teacher. Today, the people at his table.

Rashi had daughters, tradition says, and no sons. One answer to a legal question, preserved under his name, stops partway through for an apology. The writer is weak and ill, he says, and can't hold the pen himself; his daughter is writing down his words. That's how tradition reads it: a teacher in bed, and a daughter at the desk, taking down the law in her own hand. Through his daughters, his learning went on to the next generation, and the one after that. Today, Rashi's daughters.
screen: `A LETTER FROM TROYES.` → `HIS DAUGHTER HOLDS THE PEN.` → `LEARNING PASSES THROUGH THEM.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers their names as Yocheved, Miriam and Rachel. We have very little written by them or about them directly, and that silence is worth saying out loud: what women in that world knew and taught was often never written down. What we do know is the family that grew around them. Yocheved married Meir, one of Rashi's students. Their sons became great teachers in their own right. One was Samuel, known as the Rashbam, who wrote his own commentary on the Torah and wasn't shy about reading a verse differently from his grandfather. Another was Jacob, known as Rabbeinu Tam, a great teacher of law in France. These grandsons and their students began a new way of learning the Talmud. They called their notes tosafot, additions. Where Rashi explained a passage line by line, the Tosafists asked how this line fits with that one, in another tractate, and worked out contradictions, generation after generation, in schools across France and Germany. Open a printed page of the Talmud today: Rashi on the inner margin, the Tosafot on the outer, the grandfather facing the school his grandsons began. And then there are the stories. A popular one says Rashi's daughters wore tefillin. It's told and retold, but no early source says so, so tell it as a story. What the sources do show is quieter, and real: a house where learning ran through the daughters to the grandsons, and a daughter who, tradition says, could take down her father's legal answers when he could not.

936.hook: crusaders massacre the Jewish communities of the Rhineland
936.howItsDone: In Ashkenazi synagogues the memorial prayer Av HaRachamim is said after the Torah reading on Sabbaths, except on some festive ones, and some communities kept memorial books listing the names of those killed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi's daughters, and the grandsons whose additions face Rashi on the Talmud page. Your line was daughters of learning. Today we go back to the Rhine towns, and this one is hard.

On a Sabbath morning in a synagogue that follows the Ashkenazi custom, after the Torah reading, the congregation says a short memorial prayer. It begins with two Hebrew words, av harachamim, father of mercy. It asks God to remember the holy communities who gave their lives, and it doesn't name them. It doesn't need to. Tradition connects that prayer to the towns we met on the Rhine, Speyer, Worms and Mainz, and to the spring when armed bands on their way to a crusade came through them. Today's lesson is named for that year: ten ninety-six.
screen: `A SABBATH MEMORIAL PRAYER.` → `FATHER OF MERCY.` → `THE RHINE TOWNS.`

segments.voice: Our main witnesses are Hebrew chronicles written by Jews of the Rhineland, telling what happened to their own families. They read like lists and like laments at once. Bands of crusaders, and townspeople who joined them, turned on the Jewish quarters as they marched. In Speyer, the chronicles say, the bishop took the Jews under his protection, and fewer were lost there. In Worms, families who had sheltered in the bishop's palace were not safe there for long. In Mainz, the community had paid for protection, and the protection failed. Again and again the attackers offered the same choice: baptism or death. The chronicles tell of people baptized under that threat, and of others who refused, and they record both with sorrow. Tomorrow we'll look at how Jewish tradition understood those who chose to die rather than give up their faith. Today is simply for memory. The chronicles also name people who helped, a bishop who sheltered, a neighbor who hid someone; they are careful about who did what. The communities did not end. Survivors returned, and some who had been forced into baptism came home to Judaism; the rulers allowed it. Synagogues were rebuilt. Students went on studying. And the names were kept, written in memorial books and read aloud on certain Sabbaths, so that a family in a small town would not be forgotten. That is the work of memory here: not drama, not anger used as a tool, but names, said out loud.

937.title: Sanctifying the name
937.hook: sometimes by martyrdom, but usually by living so others respect God
937.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often remind people that honest business, kindness and courtesy are a Kiddush Hashem, and that dishonest conduct by a religious person is a chillul Hashem, a profaning of the name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 1096, and the Jewish towns along the Rhine. Your line was the rhineland. Today, the phrase their chroniclers used for those deaths, and the much wider meaning it carries.

A teacher hauls flax for a living, and his students want to spare him the work, so they buy him a donkey from a trader. Back home, they find a precious stone hanging from its neck. Now, they say, their teacher can stop working so hard. He asks one question. Does the seller know? No. Then take it back, he says; he bought a donkey, not a jewel. So the stone goes back, and the trader holds it and says, in effect: blessed is the God of this teacher. That moment has a name.
screen: `A DONKEY, A TRADER, A JEWEL.` → `TAKE IT BACK.` → `BLESSED IS HIS GOD.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Jerusalem Talmud, and the rabbi is Shimon ben Shetach. Kiddush Hashem means sanctifying the name, the name of God. Its opposite is chillul Hashem, profaning the name. The rabbis tie both to a verse in Leviticus, where God says: "I will be hallowed among the children of Israel." Notice where the hallowing happens: among people. Yesterday's Rhineland chroniclers used this phrase for those who died rather than give up their faith, and Jewish tradition honors them with it. Jewish law also teaches that saving a life comes first, and asks for martyrdom only in rare and terrible cases. And the rabbis teach an everyday kind too. In the Babylonian Talmud, in tractate Yoma, the sage Abaye puts it this way: let the name of Heaven become beloved because of you. Someone who studies, deals honestly in the market and speaks gently with people makes others say, how fine are this person's ways, and fortunate is the one who taught them. The reverse holds too. A person known for learning who cheats or is rude makes people think less of the teaching. So the name of God, in this view, travels with people's behavior. A returned jewel, a fair price, a kind word to a stranger: each is a small Kiddush Hashem. That is why a martyr's death and a shopkeeper's honest scale can share one phrase.

938.title: Blood libels
938.hook: false accusations beginning in Norwich led to killings; some popes condemned them
938.howItsDone: Jewish law treats gossip and talebearing (lashon hara and rechilut) as serious wrongs, and some Jews study these laws to guard what they say about others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiddush Hashem: a jewel carried back to its owner. Your line was sanctify the name by living. Today, the end of the week, and what a lie can do.

Easter week in Norwich, England. A boy named William is found dead in a wood outside the town. Nobody knows who killed him. Years later a monk named Thomas of Monmouth writes a book claiming the Jews of Norwich did it, in mockery of the crucifixion. There is no evidence. His sources are rumor, dreams and a convert's word. But the book spreads, the boy becomes a local saint, and the story finds a shape that will be told again and again in other towns.
screen: `A BOY FOUND IN A WOOD.` → `A MONK'S BOOK.` → `A STORY THAT TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: A libel is a false and damaging accusation. The blood libel is the false claim that Jews murder Christian children, and in later tellings that they use the blood in their rituals, often around Passover. Every part of it is false, and it runs straight against Jewish law, which forbids eating blood at all. The Torah repeats the ban, and the rules of kosher meat are built around removing blood. Yet the story kept returning. When a child went missing or a body was found, someone remembered the tale, and Jews were arrested, tortured into confessions, or killed by crowds. Not everyone believed it. Some popes wrote against it. Pope Innocent the Fourth, answering complaints from Jewish communities in Germany, wrote that Jews were being falsely accused of eating the hearts of murdered children, when their own law forbids such things. Some rulers issued similar protections. But a lie that people want to believe outruns a letter. The Torah has a short rule about this, in Leviticus: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." The same verse goes on to forbid standing idly by while a neighbor's blood is shed. Some readers hear the two halves together: careless words can end in harm. This week ran from riots in Spain, through Rabbeinu Gershom's rulings, Rashi and his daughters, the Rhineland and Kiddush Hashem, to this. The blood libel sits underneath much of it: a story told without evidence can cost lives.
screen: `A FALSE ACCUSATION.` · `AGAINST JEWISH LAW ITSELF.` · `SOME POPES WROTE AGAINST IT.` · then, large: `NO TALEBEARING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've heard lately about a person or a group that you can't actually check: a forwarded message, a headline, a bit of gossip. Notice the pull to repeat it, then picture letting it stop with you, not sent and not added to.
Blood libels. False stories that Jews killed children for ritual purposes, told from Norwich onward, condemned by some popes, and believed by crowds anyway. Today's word.
Your line: lies kill. And a rumor that reaches you can stop with you. See you tomorrow.
